sources.title: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022 (BBC News)
Netflix to cut about 6% of worldwide staff (NBC New York)
Netflix is laying off 6% of its workforce, 1,000 employees, in biggest round of job cuts at streaming giant in years (ABC30 Fresno, Associated Press)

chunks.text: On October 14, 2026, Netflix told its staff that it will {{lay off}} about 1,000 workers. That is around 6 percent of its [[workforce]]. It is the company's biggest round of [[job cuts]] since 2022. The news first {{came out}} in The Wall Street Journal. The company's two [[co-chief executives]] explained the cuts in a [[memo]] to staff. Most of the cuts will hit the product, technology, legal and [[human resources]] teams.

verbs.wrong: To train workers for new roles
verbs.why: Factories lay off workers when sales drop. Some companies lay off staff every winter. Netflix told its staff that it will lay off about 1,000 workers.

verbs.correct: To become known to the public
verbs.wrong: To be sent only to managers
verbs.why: The truth about a secret plan often comes out in the end. Bad news comes out fast in a small town. The news about the Netflix job cuts first came out in The Wall Street Journal.

chunks.text: "Decisions like these are never easy," the two leaders wrote. They said business is strong. Thanks to new members {{signing up}} and higher prices, Netflix's profit has grown in 2026. But the leaders said the company must be [[disciplined]] about where it puts its people and money. Netflix plans to {{go on}} investing [[heavily]] to improve its service. In 2022, it cut about 450 jobs after losing [[subscribers]] for the first time in over a decade.

verbs.correct: To join a service as a member
verbs.wrong: To watch a show for free
verbs.why: Many people sign up for the gym in January. More people sign up for a streaming service when a big show starts. New members signing up helped Netflix's profit grow in 2026.
Many people go on working after age 65. My neighbor goes on painting even though her hands hurt. Netflix plans to go on investing heavily to improve its service.

chunks.text: Growth in [[viewing time]] is slow, though. Viewing on Netflix {{went up}} only 2 percent in the [[first half]] of 2026. The company's forecast for July to September also {{fell short of}} what Wall Street expected. In late September, one of the leaders said Netflix was "not growing as fast as I want us to." [[Competition]] is growing too. Free [[platforms]] such as YouTube and TikTok keep {{drawing in}} viewers.

verbs.wrong: To be measured in a new way
verbs.why: Rents go up in big cities almost every year. The number of visitors to the beach goes up in the summer. Viewing on Netflix went up only 2 percent in the first half of 2026.

verbs.correct: To be less than what was hoped
verbs.wrong: To be the same as last year
verbs.why: Sales sometimes fall short of a company's goals. Many new restaurants fall short of what their owners hope. Netflix's forecast for July to September fell short of what Wall Street expected.
A good sale draws in a lot of shoppers. Free music in the park draws in big crowds. Free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok keep drawing in viewers.

chunks.text: In early October, Paramount {{took over}} another major Hollywood [[studio]]. Netflix had made its own [[deal]] for part of that studio, but it {{pulled out}} in February. At least one other studio has also cut jobs to {{bring down}} costs. Netflix has tried to {{branch out}} into games and [[advertising]]. But an [[analyst]] at a [[research firm]] said it has not {{come up with}} another major [[source of income]]. The cuts came six days before Netflix's [[quarterly results]] on October 20, 2026.

verbs.correct: To gain control of a company
verbs.wrong: To sell part of a company
verbs.why: A big bank often takes over a smaller one. When one company takes over another, the new owner often changes the name. In early October, Paramount took over another major Hollywood studio.

verbs.correct: To quit a deal before it is done
verbs.wrong: To sign a deal in secret
verbs.why: Some buyers pull out when the price gets too high. A team pulls out of a contest when its best player gets hurt. Netflix had made its own deal for part of that studio, but it pulled out in February.
Solar panels bring down a family's power bills. Some stores bring down their prices after Christmas. At least one other studio has also cut jobs to bring down costs.

verbs.correct: To start doing new kinds of business
verbs.wrong: To sell a business to a rival
verbs.why: Many coffee shops branch out into selling food. Some painters branch out into photography. Netflix has tried to branch out into games and advertising.

verbs.correct: To find or invent something new
verbs.wrong: To borrow more money from banks
verbs.why: Good teachers come up with fun ways to explain hard ideas. Our team comes up with new ideas every Monday. An analyst said Netflix has not come up with another major source of income.

mainIdea.s: Netflix is cutting about 1,000 jobs even though its profit is still rising. Its leaders want careful spending as viewing grows slowly and free sites like YouTube keep winning viewers.
mainIdea.why: Netflix will lay off about 6 percent of its workers while profit grows. Viewing went up only 2 percent, and free platforms keep drawing in viewers.

mainIdea.s: Netflix will remove around 6 percent of its staff because the company has started losing money. Its bosses say they will also spend less on new shows and on improving the streaming service.
mainIdea.why: Close, but Netflix's profit has grown in 2026. Its leaders said it will go on investing heavily to improve its service.

mainIdea.s: Netflix has raised the monthly price of its basic plan in the U.S. and in several other countries. The company says the extra money will pay for more live sports and new drama series.
mainIdea.why: Netflix is laying off about 1,000 workers. Viewing on the service is growing slowly, and free platforms keep drawing in viewers.

lines.text: Did you hear Netflix is going to {{lay off}} about a thousand people?
I did. [[That's rough]] for all those families.
The news {{came out}} in The Wall Street Journal first. Then the two bosses sent a memo.
Not really. Profit is up, because new people keep {{signing up}}.
Growth is slow. Viewing only {{went up}} about two percent.
So they want to [[tighten their belts]] a little.
Pretty much. But they say they'll {{go on}} investing in the service.
I watch YouTube more than Netflix these days.
You're not alone. Free sites like YouTube and TikTok keep {{drawing in}} viewers.
Are other studios cutting jobs too?
Some are. They're trying to {{bring down}} costs too. A lot of studios are [[in the same boat]].
Hasn't Netflix tried games and ads?
It has tried to {{branch out}}, but one analyst says it hasn't {{come up with}} another big way to make money.
That must be [[hard to swallow]] for the people losing their jobs.
For sure. Looking at [[the big picture]], streaming gets more crowded every year.
I'm curious to see their next results.

expressions.def: Used to show you feel sorry about someone's bad situation
ex: You lost your wallet and your keys? That's rough.

expressions.def: Used to say that people or companies spend less money than before
ex: Many families tighten their belts when food prices rise.

expressions.def: Used to say that other people have the same problem as you
ex: We all have too much homework, so we're in the same boat.

expressions.def: Used to say that something is difficult to accept
ex: The news that the store was closing was hard to swallow.

expressions.def: The whole situation, not just one small part of it
ex: Don't worry about one bad day. Think about the big picture.
